The submitted answer is "yes", and it is correct.

The question places no restriction on S, so the trivial case already works: if S contains a line, the injective curve γ(t) = (t, 0) has infinite length. Even a bounded S works. The graph of x·sin(1/x) on [0,1], with f(0) = 0, is continuous and injective, so it has no self-intersections. It lies in [0,1]×[−1,1]. Taking x_k = 2/((2k+1)π) gives f(x_k) = (−1)^k x_k, so consecutive points differ in height by x_k + x_{k+1} ≥ 2/((2k+1)π). The sum of these over k diverges, so the length is infinite. The Koch curve is a second example: it is simple, bounded, and has infinite length.
